PAGE.p: These are initial observations for the Huawei / UniVPN SSL VPN investigation in issue #603. They describe a subset exercised by a separate TCP forwarding prototype and the experimental --protocol=univpn implementation against one authorized gateway. They do not establish compatibility with all Huawei or Leagsoft firmware.

Only password authentication and IPv4 over two TLS connections were exercised. Unknown fields below retain their observed values; their semantics have not been established. Integers are in network byte order.
Following the initial request, both TLS channels use an eight-byte header followed by the indicated payload:

TLVs consist of a two-byte type, a two-byte length and that many value bytes. An interrupted or partial TLS read must retain the current frame, including when a timeout occurs immediately after its header. A new TLS record does not necessarily begin a new protocol frame.
PAGE.pre: fe fc ef be c1 92 a4 d6 00 00 00 00 00 1d 01 44 [64 zero bytes] [authentication domain, UTF-8, zero-padded to 256 bytes] 00 01 00 00
PAGE.p: The prototype requires a framed command 00 reply whose payload is four zero bytes. It then sends command 01 with a 256-byte padded domain, four zero bytes and the following TLVs:

The observed escaping replaces %, & and + with %25, %26 and %2B, respectively. The prototype uses a deterministic locally administered MAC value; requirements for that field on other gateways are unknown.

A successful command 01 response begins with a four-byte zero result. TLVs begin at byte 8 of the response payload; the first 32 bytes of type 3 supply a session token. The intervening four bytes are not interpreted. Passwords and session tokens must not be included in diagnostic reports.

Command 03 requests a virtual address, with the 32-byte token as payload. The tested successful response begins with a zero byte. Starting at payload byte 4, a type 1 TLV of length 5 contains the assigned IPv4 address in its first four bytes and an IPv4 prefix length in the fifth. A type 6 TLV contains a sequence of five-byte IPv4 network/prefix entries. Invalid prefixes and non-aligned networks are rejected. Other TLVs, including any possible DNS metadata, are not interpreted.
A second TLS connection sends command 64 with the session token. The tested response has command 64 and one zero payload byte.

tr.td: 32-byte token followed by a four-byte elapsed-millisecond counter
Eight zero bytes followed by an IPv4 packet

PAGE.p: The millisecond counter is measured since session setup and truncated to 32 bits. The prototype reads control replies while data is idle, and serializes heartbeat and packet writes on each TLS channel. Reply semantics and whether the server requires these exact intervals need further study.

On macOS, a fresh SSH connection through the prototype, binary transfers of 256 KiB in each direction, a 65-second idle SSH connection and a concurrent second connection passed. SSH host-key verification remained enabled and existing SSH multiplexed connections were not reused. A wrong TLS certificate pin was rejected before VPN authentication.

The gateway certificate did not chain to the system CA store. The live test used a first-observed full SHA-256 certificate pin; no independent verification of that initial certificate identity is claimed. A production implementation must use normal certificate validation or a pin obtained through a trusted channel.

The prototype constructs a minimal IPv4/TCP flow, not a complete TCP stack. An OpenConnect implementation should instead pass complete IPv4 packets to and from TUN and let the operating system handle TCP. It should reuse OpenConnect's certificate validation, authentication and event-loop interfaces.

The native implementation carries whole IPv4 packets over TLS; it does not implement a userspace TCP stack. Six loopback TLS integration tests cover authentication, rejected credentials, certificate trust and channel identity binding, IPv4 TCP/UDP/ICMP echo and malformed framing. These are mock tests, not evidence of all those protocols on a real gateway. Live native probes received TCP SYN-ACK and ICMP port-unreachable in response to UDP; ICMP echo did not receive a reply. System TUN/routing validation remains separate from raw packet probes.

Session tokens are bound to a live authenticated control channel. A separate --authenticate invocation followed by cookie-only startup is unsupported. Channel failure requires fresh authentication; no seamless session resumption is claimed. HTTP proxying, IPv6 and DTLS are unsupported.

A two-hour idle SSH test of the separate minimal TCP forwarder failed to resume application traffic although VPN heartbeats continued. Native and prototype long-term stability must not be inferred from heartbeat replies. Other authentication methods, firmware versions, compression, session renewal, disconnect messages and multi-hour stability remain unverified. Further redacted observations and an implementation following the existing protocol investigation guidance are welcome.
